about-text:
Welcome to *MWNF Galleries*!  
  
This is the right place if you are interested in discovering artefacts according to the material(s) they are made of or according to the type of object.  
  
In *MWNF Galleries* artefacts contributed by Partners from different countries and representing different civilisations are gathered ‘by medium’, showcasing a great variety of artistic expressions and a multitude of perceptions.  
  
After choosing a gallery from the Galleries List, you will be taken to the gallery homepage. The menu bar allows to select from different options.  
  
Within the gallery’s **Collection**, a range of filters offers different ways to explore the material. For research, you can use the **Search** bar located at the top-right of the page. If you are interested in learning about contributions from a specific institution, the **Partner** section would be the best place to start. On the **Timeline**, you will find countries’ historical context information, while **My Collection** lets you save any item from this project for later viewing.  
  
The *MWNF Galleries* database grows constantly thanks to new material added by our Partners. So please come back regularly to check for updates!  
  
Please contact the editorial team at **editing@museumwnf.net** if you experience any problems in accessing web pages or links.

exhibitionCredits:
**MWNF online Exhibition Platform**  
Under the patronage of the United Nations Alliance of Civilisations  
  
**Remarks by H.E. Mr. Miguel Ángel Moratinos**, the United Nations Under-Secretary-General holding the post of High Representative for the United Nations Alliance of Civilizations (UNAOC).  
  
I wish to wholeheartedly congratulate Museum With No Frontiers for this important milestone and for the key contribution that the new online exhibition platform will bring to the promotion of intercultural dialogue around the globe.  
  
The recent Covid-19 pandemic brought to the forefront the critical role that the online space plays in our modern world. Culture is a well-known, essential antidote to hate speech, and xenophobia, as well as to an unfounded fear of the Other rooted in a lack of understanding. Considering the prevalence of the virtual world in our daily lives, initiatives such as the one presented by Museum With No Frontiers are as urgent as they are timely. The online exhibition platform encompasses a further step towards the promotion of intercultural respect and understanding across the board, enabling both in-person and virtual dialogues that overall promote peace, respect and solidarity.

searchHowTo:
This website uses Boolean Full Text Search (FTS), which may be challenging for those who are unfamiliar with this search method. On the other hand, it enables **very accurate search results**.  
  
How to get started:  
  
First of all, if you prefer, you can search by just entering a term, and you may find the result(s) you are looking for. However, please note that no ‘refine your search’ option is available.  
  
**For multiple term searches** enter each term preceded by ‘+’ (or another operator, explained below) and separated by a space; for example, if you are looking for entries including the terms ‘prayer’, ‘rug’ and ‘Glasgow’, enter ‘+prayer +rug +glasgow’.  
  
If, for example, you are looking for entries including the terms ‘prayer’ and ‘rug’ but do not include the term ‘glasgow’, enter ‘+prayer +rug -glasgow’.  
  
**The signs ‘+’ and ‘-‘ are called ‘Operators’**. The list below explains the function of the most important ‘Operators’:  
  
**Operator: +**  
Description: a leading plus sign indicates that a word must be present in each entry that is returned.  
Example: '+ceramic +glazed' will look for entries that contain both words. '+ceramic glazed' will search for entries that contain the word 'ceramic', but list an entry higher in the results if it also contains the word 'glazed'.  
  
**Operator: -**  
Description: a leading minus sign indicates that a particular word must not be present in any of the entries that are returned. The - operator acts only to exclude results that are otherwise matched by other search terms.  
Example: '+ceramic -glazed' finds entries that contain the word 'ceramic' but not 'glazed'.  
  
**No operator:**  
Description: by default, the word is optional, but the entries that contain it are rated higher.  
Example: 'ceramic glazed' searches for entries that contain at least one of the two words.  
  
**Operator: <>**  
Description: these two operators are used to change a word's contribution to the relevance value that is assigned to an entry. The > operator increases the contribution and the < operator decreases it.  
Example: '+shape +(> ceramic < glazed)' will find entries that contain the words 'shape' and 'ceramic', or 'shape' and 'glazed', but you would see results for 'shaped ceramic ' first, followed by the 'shape glazed' results.  
  
**Operator: ~**  
Description: a leading tilde acts as a negation operator, meaning that word contributes a negative amount of importance to the entry (ranking it lower in the full list of results).  
Examples: '+shape ~ceramic' will look for entries that contain the word 'shape', but if the entry also contains the word 'ceramic', it will be listed lower than if the entry does not.  
  
**Operator:\***  
Description: the asterisk serves as the truncation (or wildcard) operator. Unlike the other operators, it is appended to the word to be affected. Words match if they begin with the word preceding the \* operator.  
Examples: 'shape\*' will return entries that contain words such as 'shape', 'shaped', 'shaping', etc.  
  
**Operator: ""**  
Description: a phrase that is enclosed within double quote ("") characters will match only the entries that contain the phrase literally, as it was entered.  
Examples: '"shaped glazed ceramic"' will return entries that contain the exact phrase "shaped glazed ceramic".  
  
If you want to learn more, please click [here](https://www.w3resource.com/mysql/mysql-full-text-search-functions.php#:~:text=Full%2DText%20Search%20in%20MySQL,based%20columns%20in%20the%20table).

thg_about_text_background:
**Background**  
  
*MWNF Galleries* build on and develop the Database of the MWNF Virtual Museums:  
  
[***Discover Islamic Art***](https://islamicart.museumwnf.org/) & [***Explore Islamic Art Collections***](https://islamicart.museumwnf.org/pm_partner_list.php?theme=EPM&type=museum)  
The *Discover Islamic Art* Virtual Museum and Virtual Exhibitions present the Islamic heritage of the Mediterranean basin, alongside collections of Islamic art hosted by the participating museums. New partners continue to enrich the *Discover Islamic Art* Database by adding new items within the follow-up project *Explore Islamic Art Collections*.  
  
[***Discover Baroque Art***](https://baroqueart.museumwnf.org/)  
The *Discover Baroque Art* Virtual Museum and Virtual Exhibitions explore the cultural environment of European Baroque, putting the spotlight on less familiar highlights of Baroque art and architecture, alongside universally known masterpieces.  
  
[***Sharing History***](https://sharinghistory.museumwnf.org/)  
The *Sharing History* Virtual Museum and Virtual Exhibitions address Arab–Ottoman–European relations in the 19th century from the specific perspectives of all parties, offering the first Database to document this period of common history.

txtTimeline:
**Have you already been at [Themes](https://exhibitions.museumwnf.org/the_use_of_colours_in_art/en/themes) to do a tour through the Exhibition?**  
  
The art world is full of colors. Color-making has its own history, rooted in places, traditions, and materiality – be it earth, stone, animals, or plants.  
  
Colors reacts to heat and light. They transform. They travel through countries and cultures. And their financial and spiritual value, often intertwined, change over time.  
  
This timeline attempts at giving a glimpse of the vast history of colors. While it does not claim to be complete, it strives to show that in any place, and at any time, humans have been looking at their environment and finding ways to create new, meaningful colors – to leave a trace of themselves.
